title: Garden Club and Hobby Shop Make a Retirement Community Unique
paras: This June we are hosting an open house to showcase our Garden Club and Hobby Shop, two amenities that consistently top the list of favorites for our residents. Both are completely free for the residents to use and each one exemplifies the community’s focus on creating a comfortable, pleasant environment.

“It’s the people here that make the difference,” said Tom, Director of the Garden Club. “Everyone here had such a diverse and interesting career. You never know who you will meet when you go to dinner.”

Tom, who taught at a university, is explaining why he and his wife Ann decided to relocate here after spending 44 years in the Washington, D.C. area. “We are truly one big, happy family,” he adds, settling into a chair underneath an umbrella.

Tom helps in keeping the Garden Club’s 24 active members organized and ensures adequate supplies are on hand. He said one of his chief concerns in leaving his home for a Life Plan Community was having outdoor space to roam and a place to get his hands dirty in the garden. “Now all I have to worry about is what to do with all these tomatoes, blueberries, potatoes and cucumbers,” he joked.

This concern about having outdoor space to plant flowers and vegetables is the reason why the Garden Club was first established and why it continues to bear the name of the resident who petitioned the board to set aside a place for the residents 10 years ago. With status as a nonprofit, the board is always looking for new ways to reinvest the community’s earnings back into refining the services and amenities it provides for its residents.

As a result, there is now a spacious, wheelchair-accessible garden area that is set on approximately a half acre of land. It is completely surrounded by a privacy fence to ward off deer and other critters attracted by the aroma of the sweet smelling flowers and vegetables. A variety of plot sizes are available, from 20’ by 20’ and 10’ by 20’ ground plots, to raised beds and table gardens, for those who have trouble squatting or spending extensive periods of time on their knees.

Tom is considering polling the members about dividing the 20’ by 20’ plots. “They are almost too big,” he laughs. “And we want to make sure there is space for everyone.” Each of the plots has access to running water and a shed for storing tools. There are even two large compost bins for the residents to share organic fertilizer. The grounds and maintenance department helps with weed control and mulching, and operations are facilitated by a memorial fund specifically set aside for the Garden Club.

A quick stroll through the garden and it’s easy to see why so many works of art were inspired by the beauty put on display by the natural world. One of those unique artists with a talent for replicating the complexity found in nature is resident Walt, who can often be found in the woodworking and hobby shop, whittling away at a block of wood. Looking at a shell with tinges of red that he recently carved from a box elder tree, it is surprising to learn the red tones are actually produced by a stress reaction the trees have to a specific type of fungus. All of Walt’s works have a shine that looks as if he’s applied a protective coat of polyurethane. In reality this comes from many, many hours of his time sanding the wood, until he finishes with a 12,000 grit sand paper and calls it done.

Fellow Craftsmen Hank and Ray are equally talented. Ray is the go-to guy in the community when furniture needs to be repaired, refurbished or simply created from scratch to the highest standards of quality and style. Hank is the artisan responsible for crafting some really intricate and cool nut crackers, which take about 20 to 25 hours each to produce.

What the guys have in common is a focus on helping others, so each piece is either donated to a local church or sold in the gift shop at a nearby care center to fund the operations there. Another common element is an appreciation for the simple fact the shop is there and filled with every tool imaginable. A relief in not having to leave anything behind is a bond they share with the members of the Garden Club. Owning a home takes work. Part of the reward is the freedom to have a garden or a workshop. Here, we constantly look for new ways to ensure our residents have access to all the comforts of home, plus world-class health care and resort-like amenities, along with the sense of being free from the drudgery of interior and exterior home maintenance.
note: Sponsored content written for the marketing director of a nonprofit continuing care retirement community. Names have been changed.

title: Chef’s Demo Showcases Quality, Diversity of Food
paras: When I point out that having a chance to sample a variety of fine cuisine is one of the best parts about working here, it is not a surprise for many people. For those who are unfamiliar with our community, the assumption is that residents and staff have access to a cafeteria, not a restaurant.

This could not be farther from the truth, however, and luckily for me, dispelling the notion is as easy as…avoiding an obvious pun. It is as simple as inviting potential residents to experience firsthand the incomparable culinary talents of our executive chef and pastry chef, which is exactly what we did recently during an exclusive, four-course demonstration.

Were the menu available to me at the time of this writing, it would certainly make for a high-quality ingredient for use in the article. That is not the case, and the fact the menu is not currently available is indicative of the exceptional quality standards in place at the restaurant, where the emphasis is on creating a farm-to-table experience and many of the menu items are constantly changing.

To put it simply, the menu here was designed to be as fresh and vibrant as our residents. Our residents are what make our community great. They bring a variety of life experiences, tastes and preferences to the table, so it just made sense that our menu would need to be as diverse as they are.

Incorporating locally-sourced ingredients of the highest possible quality, the menu here is a tasty fusion of a variety of different styles. There are four new specials every day and the menu changes every week based on the preferences of our residents and what is currently available from the local markets.

The restaurant offers Certified Angus Beef and a new Catch-of-the-Day, every day. The menu is dynamic and fluid but the favorite mainstays that many are accustomed to seeing are always available. This makes our menu an effective blend of the adventurous and the tried-and-true.

Chef Mark is far from the stereotype of the angry chef or Soup Nazi. In fact, he is patient and humble, willing to listen to feedback or seek out the preferences of our residents. Chef Mark understands that many of our residents are not Southerners, and that the ones who are from the South are always willing to try new things. This is why he characterizes his kitchen as regional, with a twist—something that is never boring and truly unlimited in its appeal.

One of the coolest things about Chef Mark is that he invites the residents to bring in their favorite recipes, so that he and the staff can prepare them for everyone. The preparation and enjoyment of food is a common, universal thread. It brings people together in ways that are impossible to describe.

Being able to share a family favorite that has been carefully refined, tested and proven over the generations is something that our residents love. Many of our residents would like to have everyone who lives here over for dinner sometime, but the cost and the clean-up prevents that from happening. Having Chef Mark prepare and serve a traditional family recipe is similar to having everyone over for dinner, with none of the downside.

It is also worth noting that our residents are encouraged to share recipes and favorite foods from all over the world. Many of our residents are extremely well-traveled, and it has become a challenge, hobby and a source of pride for them to find something new, exciting and adventurous for the chef to create.

Of course, this creates a plethora of opportunities for social engagement, a veritable smorgasbord of social interaction, something that is well known to enrich people’s lives and foster a sense of community. We believe that our restaurant sets us apart from other Life Plan Communities, and we invite you to take a private tour or sign up for our next Chef’s Demo and experience the difference.
note: Sponsored content written for the marketing coordinator of a nonprofit continuing care retirement community. Names have been changed.

title: What Does Continuing Care Actually Mean?
paras: As the marketing director of a continuing care retirement community, dispelling the myths about continuing care retirement communities is something I do on a daily basis. The concept of continuing care is simply about providing a complete, all-inclusive package of amenities, benefits and services that are designed to fit into each phase of our residents’ lives.
It’s a principle that has guided us for more than two decades and it’s been a big part of our success as the first and only not-for-profit Continuing Care Retirement Community in the area.

Ensuring that our residents have priority access to health care throughout their lives is a key component of this. With an emphasis on matching our services to the changing needs of our residents, we offer 30 days of temporary care every year at no additional cost, starting from day one.

To deliver exceptional value and added peace of mind, we provide our residents with the opportunity to use a nearby health center and an assisted living facility should they ever need it. Both are known as premier health care providers in the area.

Of course, providing a complete package of amenities and services isn’t just about delivering the highest standard of health care available in the area. It’s about providing our residents with a worry-free lifestyle that includes weekly housekeeping and linen services, building maintenance, a 24-hour security staff and emergency response system, and a host of dining options.

Making sure our residents get the most out of their retirement is paramount to what we do. After all, continuing care is about taking care of the individual as a whole. Keeping that in mind, we make every effort possible to support the physical, social, emotional and spiritual well-being of our residents. We feel that doing so is an essential element of any continuing care program.

To that end we provide the residents of our community, which spans over 60 acres, with access to a fitness center with an indoor pool, salon services, a library, woodworking shop, garden area and artists’ studio. The expansion of our community is particularly exciting. Our beautiful new apartment homes opened in January of this year; a new auditorium and a wellness center with a saltwater pool will be open soon. We are also excited about the new bar and bistro that will be completed this summer.

If this were a conversation with a potential resident, this is where the issue of costs and entrance fees would come up. The entrance fee has earned a negative reputation that is grounded in a misconception. The actual fact is that 50 to 90 percent of all the entrance fees are returned. Residents here can rest easy in the knowledge that they will always have a place to live in our community—even if their income runs out.

Many of our potential residents don’t know that a portion of the entrance fee and the monthly costs are usually tax deductible. Add to that the fact that we provide our residents with a 25 percent discount at the health center, and the result is the peace of mind that comes from having priority access to the best healthcare in the area.
note: Advertorial written for the marketing director of a nonprofit continuing care retirement community, 2015.
